{{short description|Generalization of the ice-type (six-vertex) models}}
In [[statistical mechanics]], the '''eight-vertex model''' is a generalization of the [[ice-type model|ice-type (six-vertex) models]]. It was discussed by [[T. Bill Sutherland]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Sutherland | first=Bill | title=Two‐Dimensional Hydrogen Bonded Crystals without the Ice Rule | journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics | publisher=AIP Publishing | volume=11 | issue=11 | year=1970 | issn=0022-2488 | doi=10.1063/1.1665111 | pages=3183–3186| bibcode=1970JMP....11.3183S }}</ref> and C. Fan & F. Y. Wu,<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fan | first1=Chungpeng | last2=Wu | first2=F. Y. | title=General Lattice Model of Phase Transitions | journal=Physical Review B | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=2 | issue=3 | date=1970-08-01 | issn=0556-2805 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.2.723 | pages=723–733| bibcode=1970PhRvB...2..723F }}</ref> and solved by [[Rodney Baxter]] in the zero-field case.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Baxter | first=R. J. | title=Eight-Vertex Model in Lattice Statistics | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=26 | issue=14 | date=1971-04-05 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.26.832 | pages=832–833| bibcode=1971PhRvL..26..832B }}</ref>

==Description==

As with the ice-type models, the eight-vertex model is a square [[lattice (group)|lattice model]], where each state is a configuration of arrows at a vertex. The allowed vertices have an even number of arrows pointing towards the vertex; these include the six inherited from the [[ice-type model]] (1-6), sinks (7), and sources (8).

[[File:Eightvertex2.png|thumb|The eight allowed vertices.]]

We consider a <math>N\times N</math> lattice, with <math>N^2</math> vertices and <math>2N^2</math> edges. Imposing [[periodic boundary conditions]] requires that the states 7 and 8 occur equally often, as do states 5 and 6, and thus can be taken to have the same energy. For the zero-field case the same is true for the two other pairs of states. Each vertex <math>j</math> has an associated energy <math>\epsilon_j</math> and [[Boltzmann factor|Boltzmann weight]]
:<math>
w_j=\exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon_j}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)
</math>
giving the [[partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]] over the lattice as
:<math>
Z=\sum \exp\left(-\frac{\sum_j n_j\epsilon_j}{k_\mathrm{B}T}\right)
</math>
where the outer summation is over all allowed configurations of vertices in the lattice. In this general form the partition function remains unsolved.

==Solution in the zero-field case==

The zero-field case of the model corresponds physically to the absence of external electric fields. Hence, the model remains unchanged under the reversal of all arrows. The states 1 and 2, and 3 and 4, consequently must occur as pairs. The vertices may be assigned arbitrary weights 
:<math>
\begin{align}
w_1=w_2&=a\\
w_3=w_4&=b\\
w_5=w_6&=c\\
w_7=w_8&=d.
\end{align}
</math>

The solution is based on the observation that rows in [[Transfer-matrix method (statistical mechanics)|transfer matrices]] commute, for a certain parametrization of these four Boltzmann weights. This came about as a modification of an alternate solution for the six-vertex model which makes use of [[Jacobi theta function|elliptic theta functions]].

===Commuting transfer matrices===

The proof relies on the fact that when <math> \Delta'=\Delta</math> and <math> \Gamma'=\Gamma</math>, for quantities 
:<math> 
\begin{align}
\Delta&=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2-d^2}{2(ab+cd)}\\
\Gamma&=\frac{ab-cd}{ab+cd}
\end{align}
</math>
the transfer matrices <math> T</math> and <math>T'</math> (associated with the weights <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math>, <math>d</math> and <math>a'</math>, <math>b'</math>, <math>c'</math>, <math>d'</math>) commute. Using the [[star-triangle relation]], Baxter reformulated this condition as equivalent to a parametrization of the weights given as
:<math>
a:b:c:d=\operatorname{snh}(\eta-u):\operatorname{snh} (\eta +u):\operatorname{snh} (2\eta): k\operatorname{snh} (2\eta)\operatorname{snh} (\eta-u)\operatorname{snh} (\eta+u)
</math>
for fixed modulus <math>k</math> and <math>\eta</math> and variable <math>u</math>. Here snh is the hyperbolic analogue of sn, given by
:<math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname {snh} (u) &=-i\operatorname {sn} (iu) = i\operatorname {sn} (-iu) \\
\text{where } \operatorname {sn} (u)&= \frac{H(u)}{\sqrt{k} \Theta(u)}
\end{align}
</math>
and <math>H(u)</math> and <math>\Theta(u)</math> are [[theta functions]] of modulus <math>k</math>. The associated transfer matrix <math>T</math> thus is a function of <math>u</math> alone; for all <math>u</math>, <math>v</math>
:<math>
T(u)T(v)=T(v)T(u).
</math>

===The matrix function <math>Q(u)</math>===

The other crucial part of the solution is the existence of a nonsingular matrix-valued function <math>Q</math>, such that for all complex <math>u</math> the matrices <math>Q(u), Q(u')</math> commute with each other and the transfer matrices, and satisfy
{{NumBlk|:|<math> \zeta(u)T(u)Q(u)=\phi(u-\eta)Q(u+2\eta)+\phi(u+\eta)Q(u-2\eta)</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
where
:<math>
\begin{align}
\zeta(u)&=[c^{-1}H(2\eta)\Theta(u-\eta)\Theta(u+\eta)]^N\\
\phi(u)&=[\Theta(0)H(u)\Theta(u)]^N.
\end{align}
</math>

The existence and commutation relations of such a function are demonstrated by considering pair propagations through a vertex, and periodicity relations of the theta functions, in a similar way to the six-vertex model.

===Explicit solution===

The commutation of matrices in ({{EquationNote|1}}) allow them to be [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalised]], and thus [[eigenvalues]] can be found. The partition function is calculated from the maximal eigenvalue, resulting in a [[Thermodynamic free energy|free energy]] per site of  
:<math>
\begin{align}
f=\epsilon_5-2kT\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\sinh^2((\tau-\lambda)n)(\cosh(n\lambda)-\cosh(n\alpha))}{n\sinh(2n\tau)\cosh(n\lambda)}
\end{align}
</math>
for
:<math>
\begin{align}
\tau&=\frac{\pi K'}{2K}\\
\lambda&=\frac{\pi \eta}{iK}\\
\alpha&=\frac{\pi u}{iK}
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>K</math> and <math>K'</math> are the complete elliptic integrals of moduli <math>k</math> and <math>k'</math>.
The eight vertex model was also solved in [[quasicrystals]].

==Equivalence with an Ising model==

There is a natural correspondence between the eight-vertex model, and the [[Ising model]] with 2-spin and 4-spin nearest neighbor interactions. The states of this model are spins <math>\sigma=\pm 1</math> on faces of a square lattice. The analogue of 'edges' in the eight-vertex model are products of spins on adjacent faces:
:<math>
\begin{align}
\alpha_{ij}&=\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{i,j+1}\\
\mu_{ij}&=\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{i+1,j}.
\end{align}
</math>

[[File:Isingduallattice.png|Isingduallattice]]

The most general form of the energy for this model is
:<math>
\begin{align}
\epsilon&=-\sum_{ij}(J_h\mu_{ij}+J_v\alpha_{ij}+J\alpha_{ij}\mu_{ij}+J'\alpha_{i+1,j}\mu_{ij}+J''\alpha_{ij}\alpha_{i+1,j})
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>J_h</math>, <math>J_v</math>, <math>J</math>, <math>J'</math> describe the horizontal, vertical and two diagonal 2-spin interactions, and <math>J''</math> describes the 4-spin interaction between four faces at a vertex; the sum is over the whole lattice.

[[File:Isinginteractions.png|Isinginteractions]]

We denote horizontal and vertical spins (arrows on edges) in the eight-vertex model <math>\mu</math>, <math>\alpha</math> respectively, and define up and right as positive directions. The restriction on vertex states is that the product of four edges at a vertex is 1; this automatically holds for Ising "edges." Each <math>\sigma</math> configuration then corresponds to a unique  <math>\mu</math>, <math>\alpha</math> configuration, whereas each  <math>\mu</math>, <math>\alpha</math> configuration gives two choices of <math>\sigma</math> configurations.

Equating general forms of Boltzmann weights for each vertex <math>j</math>, the following relations between the <math>\epsilon_j</math> and <math>J_h</math>, <math>J_v</math>, <math>J</math>, <math>J'</math>, <math>J''</math> define the correspondence between the lattice models:
:<math>
\begin{align}
\epsilon_1&=-J_h-J_v-J-J'-J'',\quad \epsilon_2=J_h+J_v-J-J'-J''\\
\epsilon_3&=-J_h+J_v+J+J'-J'',\quad \epsilon_4=J_h-J_v+J+J'-J''\\
\epsilon_5&=\epsilon_6=J-J'+J''\\
\epsilon_7&=\epsilon_8=-J+J'+J''.
\end{align}
</math>

It follows that in the zero-field case of the eight-vertex model, the horizontal and vertical interactions in the corresponding Ising model vanish.

These relations gives the equivalence <math>Z_I=2Z_{8V}</math> between the partition functions of the eight-vertex model, and the (2,4)-spin Ising model. Consequently a solution in either model would lead immediately to a solution in the other.
